intro.html: There are many ways to make things better. You can ease a pain without curing it, fix a mistake completely, add a finishing touch to something already good, or bring something tired back to life. Each of these ten verbs names one of those ways, and test passages love to ask which one fits.

Make a bad thing less bad: ameliorate, alleviate, mitigate. Fix it: remedy, rectify. Make a good thing better: enhance, refine, bolster (support). Bring back the life: rejuvenate (make young again), revive (make live again).

words.def: to make a bad situation better
words.ex: New streetlights helped {ameliorate} the problem of dark, lonely corners.
words.ctx: The new bus route did not end the town’s traffic problem, but it did {ameliorate} it: commutes that once took an hour now took forty minutes.
words.etym: From Latin melior, “better,” by way of French améliorer, “to improve.”

mn.cue: A MEAL-iorate: a MEAL makes it better
mn.text: Grandpa Gus is cold, tired and cranky after shoveling, until Nell brings him a hot bowl of soup. A good meal can {ameliorate} a gloomy afternoon.

scene.alt: A woman brings hot soup to a cold grandfather on a snowy bench, and he brightens up.

words.def: to make pain or trouble easier to bear
words.ex: An extra checkout lane helped {alleviate} the long lines at the store.
words.ctx: The volunteers could not end the drought, but they could {alleviate} its effects: they trucked in fresh water and shared it with every farm in the valley.
words.etym: From Latin alleviare, “to lighten”: ad (to) + levis (light).

mn.text: Kai staggers under a heavy crate until Sven lifts it onto his own broad shoulders. Taking some of the weight is a way to {alleviate} a burden.

scene.alt: A big man lifts a heavy crate off a tired boy’s hands.

words.def: to make less severe or harmful
words.ex: Planting trees along the river helped {mitigate} the spring floods.
words.ctx: The hikers could not stop the storm, but they could {mitigate} its dangers: they waited it out in a sturdy shelter and kept their extra clothes dry.
words.etym: From Latin mitigare, “to soften,” from mitis, mild, gentle.
words.note: Don’t confuse mitigate (to lessen) with militate (to work against: “The rain militated against a picnic”).

mn.cue: MITT-igate: a big MITT softens the blow
mn.text: A fast ball stings a bare hand, but a thick padded mitt softens the catch. The mitt helps {mitigate} the sting.

scene.alt: A player reaches up with a big padded mitt to catch a fast ball.

words.def: to fix or correct something that is wrong
words.ex: The mechanic {remedied} the squeak with a single drop of oil.
words.ctx: When the library learned that its ramp was too steep for wheelchairs, it moved quickly to {remedy} the problem, building a gentler ramp within a month.
words.etym: From Latin remedium, “a cure,” from mederi, “to heal,” the root of medical.
words.note: Remedy is also a noun: a cure or a fix (“a remedy for boredom”).

mn.text: The wagon wheel squeaks and wobbles until Grandpa Gus mends it with a wrench and a drop of oil. To mend what’s wrong is to {remedy} it.

scene.alt: A grandfather kneels to fix a wagon wheel with a wrench while a girl cheers.

words.ex: The store {rectified} its mistake by refunding the extra charge.
words.ctx: The newspaper had printed the wrong date for the concert, so the next morning it {rectified} the error with a notice on the front page.
words.etym: From Latin rectificare, “to make right”: rectus (straight, right) + facere (to make).

mn.text: The family photo hangs crooked, so Priya nudges it until every corner is square, like a rectangle. To set something straight is to {rectify} it.

scene.alt: A woman straightens a crooked picture frame on the wall.

words.def: to improve the quality, value or appeal of
words.ex: A pinch of salt will {enhance} the sweetness of the caramel.
words.ctx: The old photographs were faded and blurry, so the museum used careful scanning to {enhance} them; now visitors can read the shop signs in the background.
words.etym: From Old French enhaucier, “to raise,” based on Latin altus, high.

mn.cue: en-HANS: Hans adds the cherry on top
mn.text: The sundae is already good, but Hans adds whipped cream and a cherry on top. Little touches like that {enhance} it.

scene.alt: A shopkeeper named Hans holds up an ice cream with a cherry on top for a delighted girl.

words.ex: Winning the first game {bolstered} the team’s confidence.
words.ctx: Her argument was weak on its own, so she {bolstered} it with three surveys and a letter from the town engineer.
words.etym: From bolster, an old word for a long, firm pillow used to prop things up.

mn.cue: a BOLSTER is a propping PILLOW
mn.text: Granny Mae keeps slumping on the bed until Rosa props her up with a long, firm pillow called a bolster. To prop up and support something is to {bolster} it.

scene.alt: A teenager props her grandmother up in bed with a big firm pillow.

words.def: to make young, fresh or lively again
words.ex: A week at the lake {rejuvenated} the whole family.
words.ctx: The tired old park was {rejuvenated} by the neighbors’ hard work: they planted flowers, painted the benches and fixed the fountain.
words.etym: From re (again) + Latin juvenis (young), the root of juvenile.

mn.text: Grandpa Gus borrows Pip’s skateboard and rolls down the sidewalk laughing like a ten-year-old. The ride seems to {rejuvenate} him.

scene.alt: A grandfather in a helmet rides a skateboard, laughing like a kid, as his grandson cheers.

words.def: to bring back to life, strength or use
words.ex: A bucket of water {revived} the wilted tomato plants.
words.ctx: The old folk dance had nearly been forgotten, but a group of students {revived} it, learning the steps from their grandparents and performing it at the spring fair.
words.etym: From Latin revivere, “to live again”: re (again) + vivere (to live).

mn.text: The droopy flowers perk right up after Ivy gives them a long drink: they live again! Water can {revive} a wilted plant.

scene.alt: A girl waters a drooping flower, and it stands up tall and bright again.

words.def: to improve by making small changes; also, to purify
words.ex: Lila {refined} her essay through five careful drafts.
words.ctx: The first robot could barely roll across the floor, but the team kept {refining} the design, adjusting a gear here and a sensor there, until it won the contest.
words.etym: From re (again) + fine in its old sense, “to make pure.”

mn.text: Dev’s robot rolls, but it wobbles. He tightens one gear, then another, making it a little finer each time. Little by little, he will {refine} it.

scene.alt: A teen kneels and adjusts a small robot with a wrench, improving it bit by bit.

after.cap: Five ways to make things better.

after.html: Ameliorate improves a bad situation; you would not “ameliorate” a lovely party. And mitigate (to lessen) is often mixed up with militate (to work against), which is almost always followed by against.

items.q: Which sentence uses the right word?
choices: Sandbags helped mitigate the damage from the flood.
Sandbags helped militate the damage from the flood.
Sandbags helped mitigate against the flood.
items.why: Mitigate means to lessen (mitigate the damage). Militate means to work against and is used with “against.”
Ameliorate means to make a bad situation better, so it fits a problem like a water shortage.

items.q: True or false: remedy can be a noun (a cure) as well as a verb (to fix).
items.why: True. “A remedy for hiccups” is the noun; “remedy the mistake” is the verb.

items.q: The word part juven in rejuvenate means…
items.why: Juven comes from Latin juvenis, young (as in juvenile). To rejuvenate is to make young again.
